screens.title: Setting Up Your React DApp Environment for Solana
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this chapter you will set up a modern React environment tailored to Solana development and confirm that your DApp can run locally. We focus on Vite with TypeScript for fast iteration, installing the core Solana client library, and adding the Solana Wallet Adapter so users can connect wallets like Phantom. You will see how to scaffold a new project, run a local dev server, and where to place Solana-specific code. I will point out common setup pitfalls such as missing polyfills for Node. js globals and simple steps to resolve them. As a concrete example, you'll scaffold a project using the create vite command, install @solana/web3. js and the wallet adapter packages, then replace App. tsx with a minimal Hello Solana DApp component and run the dev server to verify the page loads. A common misconception is that any React starter works equally well for DApps; in practice, Vite and TypeScript reduce friction when working with blockchain data and modern bundlers handle polyfills differently. By the end of the chapter you will be able to initialize the project, add Solana libraries, and know where to troubleshoot if the browser reports missing Buffer or similar errors. Think about the first feature you'd want to wire up to a wallet connection.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn four practical skills that prepare you to build a React DApp for Solana. First, you will initialize a new React project using modern tooling, specifically Vite with a TypeScript template, and validate the dev server. This step matters because it reduces iteration time and prevents type-related bugs. Second, you will install and configure client-side Solana libraries, including the core @solana/web3. js and the Solana Wallet Adapter packages so users can connect wallets. I will explain why each package is needed and how they interact. Third, you'll understand the typical project structure for a DApp: where to keep components, hooks, and Solana-specific utilities like connection logic and constants. A clean structure makes on-chain integration maintainable. Fourth, you will be able to identify and fix common environment issues, such as missing Node. js globals in the browser, and learn the basic polyfill approach. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you know when you're ready to move on. Think of these objectives as a checklist before you write on-chain integrations.

screens.title: Scaffold a Vite React + TypeScript Project
screens.narratorSegment: Let's begin by scaffolding a project optimized for Solana front-end work. Vite offers a lightweight, fast development server and a focused build pipeline. To set up a React project with TypeScript using Vite, run the create vite command and choose the React TypeScript template. After creating the folder, change into it and run the package install command so dependencies are fetched. Finally, start the dev server to confirm the app runs locally. A concrete example is naming the project my-solana-dapp, installing packages, and confirming the default Vite welcome page appears at the provided local URL. Why this matters: a fast rebuild loop speeds wallet integration work and TypeScript reduces type errors when you later handle public keys and transaction objects. A common misconception is that create-react-app is always the safer choice; while it works, Vite reduces configuration friction and improves iteration speed. As you scaffold, watch for the terminal output that indicates the local address for the dev server. When you see the Hello Solana DApp page, you have a reliable base to add Solana libraries. What first UI will you add to your new project?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Scaffold a Vite React + TypeScript Project
Process

Create your project

A short, reliable sequence to scaffold and verify a React TypeScript starter using Vite.

Step 1 — Scaffold
Run the create vite command with the react-ts template and give the project a name.
Step 2 — Install
Change into the project folder and run the package manager install to fetch dependencies.
Step 3 — Run Dev Server
Start the development server and open the provided local URL to confirm the default page appears.
Key Takeaway

A Vite + TypeScript scaffold provides a fast, type-safe foundation for adding Solana libraries and wallet integration.

// Terminal sequence (visual example)
npm create vite@latest my-solana-dapp -- --template react-ts
cd my-solana-dapp
npm install
npm run dev
// Open the URL shown by Vite, typically a localhost address
Concrete example
Name your folder my-solana-dapp so your project name is explicit about intent.
Common mistake
Not running install after scaffolding leaves the project unable to start. Always run install before the dev server.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Minimal App.tsx — Hello Solana DApp
Code Walkthrough

A minimal App component to validate your setup

Keep the first UI simple so that later integration problems are easier to isolate.

Why this matters
A small, working UI confirms that the build and render pipeline are correct before adding wallet and blockchain logic.
Misconception
Don't add wallet adapter code until you confirm the base app loads. Mixing steps increases debugging noise.
Try this

Copy the code into src/App.tsx and reload the dev server to see the confirmation message.

// src/App.tsx
import React from 'react';
import './App.css';

function App() {
  return (
    

      

        
Hello Solana DApp!

        
Your Solana development environment is ready.

      

    

  );
}

export default App;
Concrete example: copy the snippet into src/App.tsx, save, and confirm the browser shows the header text.
Check: if the page does not render, inspect the terminal for build errors and ensure dependencies were installed.

screens.title: Core Solana Libraries to Install
screens.narratorSegment: When building a client-side Solana DApp you need a small set of libraries with distinct responsibilities. The primary library is @solana/web3. js; it provides connection objects, transaction builders, and account queries that let your app communicate with Solana clusters. Second, the Solana Wallet Adapter ecosystem includes three important packages. The adapter-react package supplies React hooks and context to manage wallet state. The adapter-react-ui package offers ready-made UI components such as a wallet button and a modal for selecting wallets. The adapter-wallets collection contains implementations for common wallets so your app can support Phantom, Solflare, and others through a shared interface. A concrete installation command installs these four packages together. A common misconception is that the wallet UI is required for web3 calls; it is not — UI packages are convenience. You can work with web3. js directly, but the adapter simplifies user sign-in and key management. After installation, confirm the new entries in package. json and that the package manager completed without errors. Which wallet would you support first in your DApp? Core Solana Libraries to Install means @solana/web3.js for blockchain calls; wallet adapters for react integration, ui components, and wallet implementations.. In practical terms, understand what each package provides and why it's required.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Core Solana Libraries to Install
Definition

What each package does

Install these packages to handle blockchain calls and wallet interactions reliably.

@solana/web3.js
Client-side API for connections, transactions, and account queries.
@solana/wallet-adapter-react
Provides React hooks and context to manage wallet state and requests.
@solana/wallet-adapter-react-ui
Pre-built UI components to let users select and connect wallets.
@solana/wallet-adapter-wallets
Collection of wallet implementations for common wallets used by DApps.
Concrete install command shown in the right panel installs all four packages at once.
// Install example (visual)
npm install @solana/web3.js \
  @solana/wallet-adapter-react \
  @solana/wallet-adapter-react-ui \
  @solana/wallet-adapter-wallets
Example: after install, inspect package.json to confirm entries for each package.
Misconception: wallet UI packages are optional; you can add them later but installing adapters early helps plan architecture.

screens.title: Wallet Adapter Integration Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating wallets in a React DApp follows a clear pattern: wrap your application with the wallet context and a modal UI provider so any component can access the connected wallet. The WalletProvider from the adapter-react package supplies hooks and context for wallet state, such as whether a wallet is connected and the public key. The WalletModalProvider from the adapter-react-ui package enables the pre-built modal and buttons to open the wallet selection UI. A typical pattern is to place these providers in src/main. tsx or src/App. tsx so the entire component tree gains wallet access. For example, you configure wallet adapters, pass them to WalletProvider, and wrap the app with WalletModalProvider. A common misconception is that wallet state should live in component-level hooks; using the adapter's provider avoids duplicating connection logic and keeps wallet interactions centralized. The concrete benefit is predictable sign-in flows and fewer edge-case errors when multiple components need to request a signature. After wrapping your app, test connecting a wallet and observing the connected public key returned by the adapter hooks. How will you present wallet state in your UI?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Wallet Adapter Integration Pattern
Architecture

Provider pattern for wallet access

Centralize wallet state and UI at the app root so all components can request signatures and read the connected public key consistently.

WalletProvider: React context and hooks for connection state and signing.
WalletModalProvider: supplies UI components like the multi-wallet button and modal.
Concrete setup
Configure wallet adapter instances, pass them to WalletProvider, and wrap your App so hooks like useWallet work across the app.
Common mistake

Placing provider wrappers inside deep components fragments wallet state. Keep providers high in the tree.

// conceptual example (not exact imports shown)
const wallets = [new PhantomWallet(), new SolflareWallet()];
Example check: after wrapping, call the adapter hook to read the public key and confirm it appears after connecting a wallet.

screens.title: Project Structure for a Solana DApp
screens.narratorSegment: A maintainable DApp separates UI concerns from blockchain logic. A recommended src layout includes folders for components, pages, hooks, services or utils for Solana-specific code, and a constants file for program IDs and cluster URLs. Components render UI and call hooks. Hooks encapsulate stateful patterns such as wallet state or form data. The services or utils folder contains connection setup, transaction builders, and program interaction functions, keeping these details out of rendering logic. Constants centralize values like program IDs and endpoints, making them easy to change per environment. For example, create src/services/connection. ts to export a function that returns a connection object configured for devnet or mainnet. A common misconception is to inline program IDs in components; doing so scatters configuration and makes updates error-prone. The practical benefit is easier testing and clear separation when you move from local development to deployed environments. Consider where you will place transaction-building helpers and name the files to reflect their role. Which helper will you create first: connection or transaction builder? Project Structure for a Solana DApp means keep components focused on rendering; place connection and transaction logic in services or utils and constants in a central file.. In practical terms, organize components, hooks, services, and constants for maintainability.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Project Structure for a Solana DApp
Hierarchy

A practical folder layout

Keep your Solana-specific logic isolated from UI code for easier maintenance and testing.

components/ — Presentational UI components and buttons.
hooks/ — Reusable React hooks for wallet-aware behavior.
services/ or utils/ — Connection setup, transaction builders, and program interactions.
constants.ts — Program IDs, cluster URLs, and static configuration.
Key Takeaway

Isolating Solana logic in services and constants keeps UI components simple and easier to reuse.

Concrete example: src/services/connection.ts exports a function createConnection that selects the cluster URL from constants and returns a connection object from web3.js.
Common mistake: hardcoding program IDs in components makes refactoring and testing difficult. Use constants instead.

screens.title: Wrapping the App with Wallet Providers
screens.narratorSegment: Now that you have the packages installed and a minimal App, wrap the application with the wallet adapter providers so wallet state is available globally. Typically this happens in the main entry file. You create an array of wallet adapter instances, pass them to the WalletProvider, and place the WalletModalProvider around your App to enable the pre-built modal UI. This pattern centralizes the wallet lifecycle and exposes hooks for connecting, disconnecting, and requesting signatures. A concrete code example is shown in the code panel. Note that autoConnect is an optional flag that attempts to reconnect a previously authorized wallet. A common misconception is that providers only affect UI components; in reality they provide the adapter hooks used by service functions to request signatures. After adding providers, test connecting a wallet and ensure the adapter hook reports the public key. If it does not, inspect the console for errors related to missing polyfills or failed imports. screens.title: Troubleshooting: The Buffer Polyfill Issue
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent browser error when using some Web3 libraries is that Buffer or other Node. js built-ins are not defined. This happens because many libraries were developed in Node. js environments where global objects such as Buffer are available. Browsers do not provide these globals, so when a library references Buffer at runtime the console throws an error. Modern bundlers like Vite often polyfill common modules automatically, but not always. The typical solution is to install a browser-compatible buffer package and configure the bundler to provide it as a global. For example, installing the buffer package and shimming it in the bundler config resolves the missing Buffer error in many setups. A common misconception is that reinstalling the library will fix a Buffer error; it usually requires a bundler or polyfill change. Compare the two scenarios: when the Buffer polyfill is present, web3. js functions run; when it is missing, connection setup or transaction serialization fails. After applying a polyfill, reload the page and confirm the console no longer reports missing globals. Which polyfill will you try first if you see Buffer not defined?

screens.narratorSegment: Dependency mismatches and version conflicts commonly interrupt DApp setup. After adding libraries, always inspect package. json to confirm versions and run a fresh install if you edit dependencies manually. Another pitfall is adding packages without checking compatibility with your toolchain; some older libraries expect a Node. js runtime and require polyfills when used in the browser. A frequent browser error when using some Web3 libraries is that Buffer or other Node. js built-ins are not defined. This happens because many libraries were developed in Node. js environments where global objects such as Buffer are available. Browsers do not provide these globals, so when a library references Buffer at runtime the console throws an error. Modern bundlers like Vite often polyfill common modules automatically, but not always. The typical solution is to install a browser-compatible buffer package and configure the bundler to provide it as a global. For example, installing the buffer package and shimming it in the bundler config resolves the missing Buffer error in many setups. A common misconception is that reinstalling the library will fix a Buffer error; it usually requires a bundler or polyfill change. Compare the two scenarios: when the Buffer polyfill is present, web3. js functions run; when it is missing, connection setup or transaction serialization fails.
